#13. Internal Memorandum
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nAn internal memorandum from a classified archive. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,240,190,70]TOP SECRET. Copy No. 2.%c[255,216,186,140]
From the research plan for 1986.
 
Continue studying the persistence of implanted directives after exposure has ended. The primary objective is to maintain obedience without direct contact with the operator.
 
Establish a separate group of minors for long-term observation.
 
In unclassified medical records, use the designation "Restorative Adaptation Programme".
 
Do not include the true objectives of the work in patient records.
#14. Evacuation List Attachment
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nAn attachment to an evacuation list, with a note on the back. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,240,190,70]EVACUATION POINT No. 4. 28 April 1986.%c[255,216,186,140]
 
Transfer to the special medical team:
 
Sergey Pavlovich Berestov — E-17/45.
Anton Pavlovich Berestov — E-17/46.
 
Transfer without family accompaniment. Inform their mother, Irina Petrovna Berestova, that the children will only be away for an examination. Do not enter the receiving institution's address in the general register.
 
Pencilled on the back: "Berestova has come back for the second day running. She's demanding to see her sons. Who's supposed to answer her?"
#15. Initial Examination Report
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nA sheet recording the results of an initial medical examination. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,240,190,70]GROUP E-17. 29 April 1986.%c[255,216,186,140]
 
E-17/45: high susceptibility to suggestion. Retains implanted directives on repeat testing. Recommended for the long-term programme.
 
E-17/46: inconsistent results. Does not follow instructions reliably and repeatedly asks about his older brother. Not recommended for the main group.
 
Keep both in the ward pending a decision by the commission. All information provided to relatives must come from the group supervisor.
 
Major A. R. Kostin, Medical Service.
#16. Grounds for Separation
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nA signed internal directive. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,240,190,70]Appendix to the directive concerning Group E-17.%c[255,216,186,140]
 
When the two are housed together, E-17/45 stops following previously reinforced instructions. Addresses the younger subject by name and demands to be returned to their mother. Contact with the operator is restored once E-17/46 is removed.
 
The family bond is obstructing further work.
 
House the subjects separately. Prohibit correspondence and visits. Do not record their relationship in the new personal files.
 
A. R. Kostin.
#17. Complications Report
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nA page from a medical log with the doctor's signature crossed out. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,240,190,70]From the initial examination log.%c[255,216,186,140]
 
Following preliminary trials, E-17/46 exhibits memory loss. Unable to give his home address. Recognises his mother in a photograph but cannot recall her name. Cries when staff attempt to continue the examination.
 
I recommend that the procedures be stopped and the child returned to the adult accompanying him.
 
The doctor's signature has been crossed out.
 
Below: "Return not authorised. Keep under observation. In the general medical record, attribute these findings to earlier trauma."
#18. Transfer Cover Sheet
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nA covering sheet from an old personal file. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,240,190,70]For the transfer of a child to an orphanage.%c[255,216,186,140]
 
E-17/46. Referred following a prolonged stay at a specialised institution. Prepare identity documents using his latest registration details.
 
Enter in the unclassified file: "No information available on relatives. Does not recall his early childhood."
 
Do not forward the original admission records to the receiving institution.
 
In the margin: "Asked whether anyone would come for him. The papers being forwarded list no one who could give him an answer."
#19. Discharge Report
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nA discharge report with an enclosed note. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,240,190,70]Due to cuts in funding.%c[255,216,186,140]
 
Release E-17/45. Issue civilian identity documents under his most recently registered name.
 
Continues to report sleep and memory disturbances. No grounds found for extending his stay.
 
If asked about his family, state that his younger brother is dead and his mother's whereabouts are unknown.
 
Enclosed note: "Subject has requested his brother's death certificate. Request denied. Do not respond to any further requests."
#20. Research Materials Transfer Record
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nA record of the transfer of research materials, with an enclosed sheet. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,240,190,70]Group E-17 archive. Appendix to the institution's closure inventory.%c[255,216,186,140]
 
Transfer the suggestion protocols, observation logs and research on retained directives to the team continuing the work.
 
Closing the institution does not mean ending the work.
 
A sheet from a later date is attached:
 
"Include the E-17 materials in programme %3#w%2a. Begin trials using a single source of influence for the group. Exclude direct contact with the operator.
 
During preliminary testing, subjects describe the instructions as a voice whose origin they cannot explain. Some insist they have always heard it."
#21. A Page from Sergey's Notebook
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nA page from Sergey's personal notebook. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,216,186,140]Found another letter from Mum. She was looking for both of us. If they lied to her the way they lied to me, Anton might still be alive.
 
Heard that voice again in the city centre. Couldn't make out the words. When we were children, hearing it always meant an order was coming.
 
Was about to leave, then found myself outside another building. Don't remember getting there.
 
Writing this down while I still remember my own name. Sergey Berestov. Need to find out about my brother.
#22. After the Signal Ceased
%c[255,240,190,70]Important clue%c[255,216,186,140]\n \nAn excerpt from a field journal, with a conclusion drawn from archival records. The full text is available in the encyclopedia.

%c[255,240,190,70]From a field observation journal. Appendix to archive E-17.%c[255,216,186,140]
 
The men report that they can no longer hear the Voice. Some still stand guard and gather to pray. There are no orders, but the routine continues.
 
One remembered the name of his street. Another refused to discuss his past and insisted that we stop using his former name.
 
Ending the exposure does not restore lost memories.
 
Today, for the first time, one of them asked if he was allowed to leave. The others said nothing for a long time. Then they stepped aside to let him pass.
 
Conclusion drawn from the archival records.
 
The stated aim of the USSR's "Monolith" programme — sustained obedience after exposure ends — has not been achieved. The subjects have resumed making independent decisions, including refusing to perform duties they had been conditioned to accept.
 
The programme must be deemed a failure. Memory impairment and the effects of prolonged exposure persist. The programme documentation makes no provision for assistance to the subjects.
Talk to Your Brother
It's been long enough. I should go back and talk things over with my brother.
Help Your Brother Recover His Memory
Sergey doesn't remember our conversation. I need to find something that will help him remember and make sense of our past.
Show the Records to Your Brother
Now it all makes sense. We were separated deliberately. I should show my brother the documents I've found. Maybe they'll help bring him back to himself.
Sergey, can we talk?
How do you know my old name? No one knows it.
Wait, you don't remember me? We talked the other day.
Sorry, I don't remember. Was it something important?
It was very important. What's happening...? What do you actually remember?
I remember the silence. I had a purpose, a mission I had to complete at any cost. And I remember... being somewhere else, then finding myself here... Strange. I've always been here.
I need to find something that'll help you remember.
Did you say something?
No, it's nothing. I have to go, but I'll be back soon. Just don't go anywhere.
Very well, Brother. Such is the will of the Monolith.
Yes, Brother...
I know what happened... You need to see this.
Hello. Take a seat... What did you want to talk about?

Find an Outfit for Sergey

The documents helped Sergey recognise me and piece together some of his past. He's agreed to move to Yanov Station, but his Monolith armour would give him away. I need to bring him a spare outfit — anything except Monolith gear. I'm keeping the one I'm wearing. Whatever I give him is what he'll be wearing when he arrives at Yanov. He's waiting by the campfire.
I found some records. I think things are finally starting to make sense.
What records?
From a secret facility. They were trying to suppress people's will and plant commands in their minds. You and I were part of those experiments, Sergey. We were just children.
What were they trying to achieve?

They wanted people to think an order was their own idea, and keep obeying even after the conditioning stopped. Later, they handed the research over to another team. In those new trials, everyone got their instructions from the same source: a voice they could all hear.
Wait… Go on.

They said I wasn't suitable. The suggestions didn't stick. But you kept following their instructions. Except when I was with you: you'd ask about Mum and stop obeying. That's why they separated us. Then they sent me to an orphanage and removed all mention of our family from my papers.
You're talking about us?
Do you recognise me?
I remember you coming to see us before. Anton, isn't it?
Not again... Here, read it for yourself. Those are our names. And this is your notebook.\n \n(Holds out the documents.)

(Sergey silently leafs through the papers for a long time.)\n \nAntoshka... I'm starting to remember... Yes, that's my handwriting. And I was looking for you? Yes... I was. Then why did I end up here?
I don't know, brother. Can you remember anything else?

Bits and pieces. Clean rooms. Almost empty: a bed, a table, a lamp. And a voice. It told me when to get up, where to look, what to say. Sometimes I'd think I'd decided to do something myself. Then it would say exactly the same thing.
The records mention the rooms and the voice. What happened after that? How did you get out?

There were fewer and fewer of us. Then they moved us to another building and stopped calling us in for sessions. One day they gave us clothes and papers. It wasn't my surname on the papers, but I got used to that, too. They told us, "The observation period is over. You're free to go"... Then I remember the gates and the road. By then I was a grown man, but I had nowhere to go.

The papers say their funding was cut. They let you go and told you your younger brother was dead and your mother was missing. But they were lying. She was looking for both of us, coming back and demanding that they return her sons.\n \nI spent all those years without knowing, too...

They told me you'd died... And at first I believed them. But I still had your pendant. It was as though it kept telling me to go back to the city and find you. Sometimes I dreamt of a boy who called me Cricket. I couldn't remember his face, just his voice.
Is that why you came back to Pripyat?

I wanted to find our home, the evacuation lists... anyone who remembered our family. I thought if I came back, I'd remember everything. But when I got to the centre, I heard the Voice again. It was so familiar... All at once I knew where to go and what to do. Just like in those rooms.
And you forgot why you'd come back?

Looks that way. I remember the weapon in my hands, the unfamiliar faces, the prayers. We all did the same things, and it felt like it'd always been that way. But sometimes something came back to me. I wrote it down while I still could. These pages prove it... I was still trying to find you after all.
So you remember now?
Not all of it. I know who you are. I remember the pendant, but our childhood only comes back in pieces. The moment I try to follow one of those memories, it all starts to fall apart.
What are we going to do now?
I don't know, Anton. My head's splitting. We should probably get out of here. But how can I leave my brothers behind?
Sergey, they're not your brothers. You've only got one real brother, and he's standing right in front of you. Me.

Don't say that. You're my own flesh and blood. I'm glad you're alive, and I'm grateful for everything you've done. But they're like me. Some of them can't even remember their own names. We held on to each other when we had nothing else. I can't just turn my back on them. Do you understand?

I do. Then let's start with you. There's a station south of the city: Yanov. I'm not asking you to forget those people, but could you at least move somewhere safer? You're out in the open here. Someone might come looking for payback over what you did.
You think they'll let me stay at the station?
I can't speak for everyone. But you'll be coming in peace, and I'll be there. That's better than staying here and waiting for someone to recognise that uniform.
You're probably right. I could stay there for a while. But how am I supposed to go anywhere in this armour? It's our symbol, and it makes us an easy target for every infidel... I mean, everyone else.
I'll find you a regular stalker outfit. We'll meet at Yanov after that. All right? Just wait here for now. Don't go off on your own.
Deal. I'll wait. Take the records back. Keep them with you.\n \nAnton... Thank you, brother.
I'll be back soon.
Here, take the %s.
(condition: %d%%)
Thanks, brother. Give me a little time and I'll come to Yanov.
All right. I'll be waiting.
I have to go.
You don't have that outfit with you. Bring me another one, brother.
All right. I'll bring one later.

Sergey Sverchkov. After meeting Anton, he left Pripyat and settled at Yanov.
Hello, brother.
Hey, you made it. Thanks.
I'm the one who should be thanking you for helping me remember who I am. I'll stay here for a while.
All right. I've still got a few things to take care of.
